Let $d\ge1$ and let $U$, $M$, $V$, $A$, $B$, $H=A+B$, $D_h$, $K_h$ and $V_h$ be as in [[def-cm-splitting-hamiltonian-and-verlet-map]]. Let $W\subseteq U$ be open, bounded and convex, let $K\subseteq W$ be nonempty compact, and let $r>0$ satisfy $K+\overline B_r(0)\subseteq W$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). Put

$$X_H(q,p):=(M^{-1}p,\,-\nabla V(q)),\qquad M_0:=\sup_W\lVert X_H\rVert,\quad L_1:=\sup_W\lVert DX_H\rVert,\quad L_2:=\sup_W\lVert D^2X_H\rVert,$$

the derivatives being the total derivatives with operator norms ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]); assume all three numbers are finite (for example, this holds when $\overline W\subseteq U$). Let $\Phi_t$ be the local flow of $X_H$ ([[def-cm-local-flow-of-an-autonomous-system]]).

Then there exist $h_0>0$ and $C<\infty$, depending only on $d$, $r$, $\lVert M^{-1}\rVert$, $\sup_K\lVert p\rVert$, $M_0$, $L_1$ and $L_2$, such that for every $(q,p)\in K$ and every $0<|h|\le h_0$:

1. $\Phi_h(q,p)$ is defined and lies in $W$, and
 $$\Bigl\lVert\Phi_h(q,p)-(q,p)-hX_H(q,p)-\tfrac{h^2}{2}DX_H(q,p)X_H(q,p)\Bigr\rVert\le C|h|^3.$$
2. $V_h(q,p)$ is defined and lies in $W$, and its two block components satisfy
 $$V_h(q,p)=\Bigl(q+hM^{-1}p-\tfrac{h^2}{2}M^{-1}\nabla V(q)+\rho_1,\;\; p-h\nabla V(q)-\tfrac{h^2}{2}H_V(q)M^{-1}p+\rho_2\Bigr)$$
 with $\lVert\rho_1\rVert,\lVert\rho_2\rVert\le C|h|^3$; equivalently $V_h$ and $\Phi_h$ have the same expansion through order two,
 $$X_H(q,p)=\bigl(M^{-1}p,\,-\nabla V(q)\bigr),\qquad DX_H(q,p)X_H(q,p)=\bigl(-M^{-1}\nabla V(q),\,-H_V(q)M^{-1}p\bigr).$$
3. Consequently $\lVert V_h(q,p)-\Phi_h(q,p)\rVert\le C|h|^3$ for every $(q,p)\in K$ and $0<|h|\le h_0$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]. Read the autonomous system

$$x'(t)=F(x(t))$$

as the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] with domain $D=\mathbb R\times U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ and right-hand side $(t,x)\mapsto F(x)$. Its initial value problems satisfy the Picard-Lindelöf hypotheses, so by [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] every $a\in U$ has a unique maximal solution.

For $a\in U$ denote by

$$x(\,\cdot\,;a):I_a\longrightarrow U$$

the unique maximal solution with $x(0;a)=a$, where $I_a\subseteq\mathbb R$ is its maximal interval of existence ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]]); $I_a$ is an open interval containing $0$, and every solution of $x'=F(x)$ through $(0,a)$ is a restriction of $x(\,\cdot\,;a)$.

The **flow domain** of $F$ is the set

$$\Omega:=\{\,(t,a)\in\mathbb R\times U\;:\;t\in I_a\,\},$$

and the **local flow** (also **phase flow**) of $F$ is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow U,\qquad \Phi(t,a):=x(t;a).$$

For $t\in\mathbb R$ the **time-$t$ map** is the partial map

$$\Phi_t:\Omega_t\longrightarrow U,\qquad \Omega_t:=\{\,a\in U:(t,a)\in\Omega\,\},\qquad \Phi_t(a):=\Phi(t,a).$$

Thus $\Phi_0(a)=a$ whenever it is defined, and $(t,a)\in\Omega$ exactly when the maximal solution of $x'=F(x)$ through $a$ is defined at time $t$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: Exact-flow stability. Write $a=|h|$. For short trajectories starting at $x,y\in K_1$, their distance $u(t)$, with time oriented by the sign of $h$, satisfies $u(t)\le u(0)+L\int_0^tu(s)ds$ on $0\le t\le a$ by [F2]. If $v(t)=u(0)+L\int_0^tu(s)ds$, then $v'\le Lv$; differentiation of $e^{-Lt}v(t)$ proves $v(t)\le e^{Lt}u(0)$. Thus $\|\Phi_h(x)-\Phi_h(y)\|\le e^{La}\|x-y\|$.

Recurrence. Set $e_j=\|z_j-y_j\|$. By the flow composition law and [F1], $e_{j+1}\le\|V_h(z_j)-\Phi_h(z_j)\|+\|\Phi_h(z_j)-\Phi_h(y_j)\|\le C_1a^3+e^{La}e_j$. Since $e_0=0$, induction gives $e_n\le C_1a^3\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}e^{Lak}$.

Evaluation. For $L>0$ the sum is $(e^{Lna}-1)/(e^{La}-1)$, and $e^{La}-1\ge La$, obtained by integrating $Le^{Lt}\ge L$ on $[0,a]$. Hence $e_n\le C_1a^2(e^{LT}-1)/L$. For $L=0$ the sum equals $n$ and $na\le T$ gives $e_n\le C_1Ta^2$.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{2d}$ be a phase domain with coordinates $z=(q,p)$, $q=(q^1,\dots,q^d)$ and $p=(p_1,\dots,p_d)$, standard two-form $\omega_U=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ and standard symplectic matrix $J$ ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]).

Fix a matrix $M\in M_d(\mathbb R)$ that is **symmetric and positive definite**, meaning $M^{\mathsf T}=M$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]) and $v^{\mathsf T}Mv>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^d$; here $v^{\mathsf T}Mv$ is the matrix product of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Fix an open $\Pi\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ with $U\subseteq\Pi\times\mathbb R^d$ and a function $U_{\mathrm{pot}}:\Pi\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^3$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), whose gradient $\nabla U_{\mathrm{pot}}$ and Hessian matrix $H_{U_{\mathrm{pot}}}$ are those of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]; write $\nabla U_{\mathrm{pot}}(q)$ as a column vector and abbreviate $U_{\mathrm{pot}}(q)$ by $V(q)$ on $U$.

On $U$ define the **kinetic part** and **potential part**

$$A(q,p):=\tfrac12\,p^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}p,\qquad B(q,p):=V(q),\qquad H:=A+B,$$

and the **drift** and **kick** maps $D_h,K_h:U\to\mathbb R^{2d}$,

$$D_h(q,p):=(q+h\,M^{-1}p,\;p),\qquad K_h(q,p):=(q,\;p-h\,\nabla V(q)).$$

Both are defined wherever their displayed values lie in $U$; in particular $D_h$ is defined on $U$ whenever $(q+hM^{-1}p,p)\in U$, and $K_h$ on $U$ whenever $(q,p-h\nabla V(q))\in U$. The **velocity-Verlet map** of the splitting $H=A+B$ at step $h\in\mathbb R$ is the composite

$$V_h:=K_{h/2}\circ D_h\circ K_{h/2},$$

defined on the set of $(q,p)\in U$ for which the composition exists and its value lies in $U$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $U$, $M$, $V$, $A$, $B$, $H=A+B$, $D_h$, $K_h$ and $V_h$ be as in [[def-cm-splitting-hamiltonian-and-verlet-map]], with $\omega_U$ the standard two-form and $J=\begin{pmatrix}0_d&I_d\\-I_d&0_d\end{pmatrix}$ the standard symplectic matrix ([[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]). Then, on the sets where the maps are defined:

1. $D_h$ is $C^\infty$ with constant derivative
 $$DD_h(q,p)=\begin{pmatrix}I_d&hM^{-1}\\0_d&I_d\end{pmatrix},$$
 and $D_h$ is the time-$h$ map of the local flow ([[def-cm-local-flow-of-an-autonomous-system]]) of the Hamiltonian field $X_A(q,p)=(M^{-1}p,0)$ of the kinetic part; moreover
 $$DD_h(q,p)^{\mathsf T}J\,DD_h(q,p)=J.$$
2. $K_h$ is $C^2$ with derivative
 $$DK_h(q,p)=\begin{pmatrix}I_d&0_d\\-h\,H_V(q)&I_d\end{pmatrix},$$
 where $H_V$ is the Hessian matrix of $V$, and $K_h$ is the time-$h$ map of the local flow of the Hamiltonian field $X_B(q,p)=(0,-\nabla V(q))$ of the potential part; moreover
 $$DK_h(q,p)^{\mathsf T}J\,DK_h(q,p)=J.$$
3. Wherever $V_h$ is defined and $C^1$, its derivative satisfies
 $$DV_h(q,p)^{\mathsf T}J\,DV_h(q,p)=J,$$
 so that $V_h^*\omega_U=\omega_U$: the velocity-Verlet map preserves the standard two-form and is a local symplectomorphism.

derivations.claim: Matrix and invariant. Multiplying the three displayed shear matrices gives $S_h$ as stated. Direct multiplication gives $S_h^{\mathsf T}\operatorname{diag}(\alpha,1)S_h=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha,1)$, using $(1-h^2/2)^2+h^2\alpha=1$. Thus $I_h(z_n)=I_h(z_0)$ and $q_j^2\le2I_h(z_0)/\alpha$.

Original energy and boundary. Since $H-I_h=h^2q^2/8$, $|H(z_n)-H(z_0)|=(h^2/8)|q_n^2-q_0^2|\le h^2I_h(z_0)/(4\alpha)$. At $h=2$ the invariant matrix is singular. For $h>2$, $\det S_h=1$ and $\operatorname{tr}S_h=2-h^2<-2$, so the real reciprocal eigenvalues have one modulus greater than one. This explains the step restriction without asserting stability at its excluded endpoint.

Let $m\ge1$, let $a\in\mathbb C^m$, let $\rho$ be a polyradius with $0<\rho_k<\infty$, and let $f:\Delta_\rho(a)\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and holomorphic in each variable separately, that is, for every $k$ and every choice of the other coordinates the slice $\zeta\mapsto f(\dots,\zeta,\dots)$ is holomorphic on its open disc ([[def-cm-complex-phase-domains-and-holomorphic-maps]], [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]). For a polyradius $r$ with $r_k<\rho_k$ put $M(r):=\sup_{\Gamma_r(a)}|f|$, a finite number.

Then:

1. **Iterated Cauchy formula.** For every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$,
 $$f(z)=\frac{1}{(2\pi i)^m}\oint_{|\zeta_1-a_1|=r_1}\cdots\oint_{|\zeta_m-a_m|=r_m}\frac{f(\zeta)}{\prod_{k}(\zeta_k-z_k)}\,d\zeta_1\cdots d\zeta_m,$$
 and the iterated integrals in any order of the variables agree.
2. **Power-series expansion.** For every polyradius $r'$ with $r_k<r'_k<\rho_k$, and every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$,
 $$f(z)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N^m}c_\alpha\,(z-a)^\alpha,\qquad c_\alpha=\frac{1}{(2\pi i)^m}\oint_{\Gamma_{r'}(a)}\frac{f(\zeta)\,d\zeta}{(\zeta-a)^{\alpha+\mathbf 1}},$$
 where the coefficients $c_\alpha$ do not depend on $r'$, the series converges absolutely and uniformly on every compact subset of $\Delta_\rho(a)$, and $|c_\alpha|\le M(r')\prod_k (r'_k)^{-\alpha_k}$.
3. **Holomorphy, derivatives and estimates.** The function $f$ is holomorphic on $\Delta_\rho(a)$ in the sense of [[def-cm-complex-phase-domains-and-holomorphic-maps]]. Its coordinate derivatives $\partial_{z_k}f$ exist everywhere on $\Delta_\rho(a)$, are continuous and holomorphic in each variable separately there, and satisfy, for $0<s_k<\rho_k$,
 $$|\partial_{z_k}f(a)|\le\frac{M(s)}{s_k}.$$

Let $m,l,p\ge1$ and let $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$, $D'\subseteq\mathbb C^l$ be open, with holomorphy in the sense of [[def-cm-complex-phase-domains-and-holomorphic-maps]].

1. **Chain rule.** If $g:D'\to D$ and $F:D\to\mathbb C^p$ are holomorphic, then $F\circ g:D'\to\mathbb C^p$ is holomorphic and
 $$D(F\circ g)(z)=DF\bigl(g(z)\bigr)\circ Dg(z)\qquad(z\in D').$$
2. **Wirtinger derivatives and the bracket matrix.** If $f:D\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, then $f$ is totally differentiable as a map of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ and, writing $x_k,y_k$ for the real and imaginary parts of $z_k$,
 $$\partial_{\bar z_k}f:=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_{x_k}f+i\,\partial_{y_k}f\bigr)=0,\qquad \partial_{z_k}f:=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_{x_k}f-i\,\partial_{y_k}f\bigr)=Df(e_k).$$
 Consequently, for holomorphic $f,g$ on a complex phase domain $D\subseteq\mathbb C^{2d}$, with $\nabla f=(\partial_{z^1}f,\dots,\partial_{w_d}f)$ and $J$ the standard matrix,
 $$\{f,g\}=(\nabla f)^{\mathsf T}J\,\nabla g.$$
3. **Coefficient extraction in a complex step variable.** Let $0<\sigma\le\infty$ and let $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, and let $F:\{|h|<\sigma\}\times D\to\mathbb C^p$ be holomorphic. Then for every $j\in\mathbb N$ the coefficient map
 $$c_j(z):=\partial_h^jF(0,z)/j!$$
 is holomorphic on $D$, and for every $0<s<\sigma$, $c_j(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|h|=s}\frac{F(h,z)}{h^{j+1}}\,dh$.
4. **Locally uniform limits.** If $F_n:D\to\mathbb C^p$ are holomorphic and $F_n\to F$ locally uniformly on $D$ in the sense of [[rem-locally-uniform-convergence-dictionary]] and [[def-uniform-convergence-of-complex-valued-functions]], then $F$ is holomorphic on $D$.

Let $a\le b$ be real, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, and let $\varphi:[a,b]\times\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be jointly continuous. Suppose $\varphi(t,\cdot)$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$ for every $t\in[a,b]$. Then the componentwise Riemann integral

$$F(z):=\int_a^b\varphi(t,z)\,dt$$

is holomorphic on $\Omega$.

If, in addition, $\partial_z\varphi(t,z)$ exists everywhere and is jointly continuous on $[a,b]\times\Omega$, then

$$F'(z)=\int_a^b\partial_z\varphi(t,z)\,dt.$$

If $\varphi:[a,b]\times\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is jointly continuous and $\varphi(t,\cdot)$ is holomorphic for every $t$, then $F(z)=\int_a^b\varphi(t,z)\,dt$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. If continuous functions $f_n:X\to\mathbb C$ converge uniformly to $f:X\to\mathbb C$ in the sense of [[def-uniform-convergence-of-complex-valued-functions]], then $f$ is continuous.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let each $f_n:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose $f_n\to f$ locally uniformly on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[rem-locally-uniform-convergence-dictionary]]. Then $f$ is holomorphic and

$$f_n^{(k)}\longrightarrow f^{(k)}$$

locally uniformly on $\Omega$ for every natural $k$, with $f^{(0)}=f$.

A locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, and for every natural $k$ the $k$th derivatives converge locally uniformly to the $k$th derivative of the limit.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

**Holomorphic maps.** Let $m,p\ge1$ and let $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, identified with an open subset of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ through $\mathbb C^m\cong\mathbb R^{2m}$. A map $F:D\to\mathbb C^p$ is **complex differentiable at** $a\in D$ when there is a map $L:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C^p$ that is $\mathbb C$-linear — $L(u+v)=L(u)+L(v)$ and $L(\lambda u)=\lambda L(u)$ for $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ ([[def-linear-map]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) — with

$$F(a+v)=F(a)+L(v)+r(v),\qquad \frac{\lVert r(v)\rVert}{\lVert v\rVert}\longrightarrow0\ \ (v\to0),$$

the norm being the Euclidean norm of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ and $\mathbb R^{2p}$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]). Such an $L$ is unique by the argument of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]], applied componentwise; it is denoted $DF(a)$. The map $F$ is **holomorphic on** $D$ when it is complex differentiable at every point of $D$; for $m=p=1$ this is the notion of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]. For holomorphic $F$ and $k\le m$ put $\partial_{z_k}F(a):=DF(a)(e_k)$, the $k$-th coordinate derivative; for $p=1$ this is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] in the complex coordinate direction.

**Real analytic functions.** Let $N\ge1$ and let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^N$ be open. A function $\varphi:V\to\mathbb R$ is **real analytic at** $x\in V$ when there are an open set $W\subseteq\mathbb C^N$ with $x\in W$ and a holomorphic $F:W\to\mathbb C$ with $F(\xi)=\varphi(\xi)$ for every $\xi\in W\cap V$; $\varphi$ is **real analytic on** $V$ when it is real analytic at every point of $V$. Thus real analyticity is defined here exactly as *admitting a local holomorphic extension*.

**Polydiscs.** For $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $\rho=(\rho_1,\dots,\rho_m)$ with $0<\rho_k\le\infty$ put

$$\Delta_\rho(a):=\{\,z\in\mathbb C^m:\ |z_k-a_k|<\rho_k\ \text{for all }k\,\},\qquad \Gamma_\rho(a):=\{\,z:\ |z_k-a_k|=\rho_k\ \text{for all }k\,\},$$

the open **polydisc** and its **distinguished boundary**; a polydisc is open and convex ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metric-topology]]).

**Complex phase domains.** Let $d\ge1$. A **complex phase domain** is a nonempty open $D\subseteq\mathbb C^{2d}$ whose points are written $Z=(z,w)$ with $z=(z^1,\dots,z^d)$, $w=(w_1,\dots,w_d)\in\mathbb C^d$. On it define the **complexified canonical two-form** and the **complexified Poisson bracket** of holomorphic functions $f,g:D\to\mathbb C$ by

$$\omega_{\mathbb C}:=\sum_{i=1}^d dz^i\wedge dw_i,\qquad \{f,g\}:=\sum_{i=1}^d\bigl(\partial_{z^i}f\,\partial_{w_i}g-\partial_{w_i}f\,\partial_{z^i}g\bigr),$$

and for a holomorphic $f:D\to\mathbb C$ its **complex Hamiltonian field** $X_f:=J\nabla f$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0_d&I_d\\-I_d&0_d\end{pmatrix}$ is the standard symplectic matrix of [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]] and $\nabla f=(\partial_{z^1}f,\dots,\partial_{z^d}f,\partial_{w_1}f,\dots,\partial_{w_d}f)$ is the gradient column of coordinate derivatives. The real subspace $\mathbb R^{2d}\subseteq\mathbb C^{2d}$ and the restriction of $\omega_{\mathbb C}$, $J$ and $\{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\}$ to real-valued functions reproduce the real objects of [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]].

**Distance domains.** For $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{2d}$ and $r>0$ put

$$D(r):=\{\,\zeta\in\mathbb C^{2d}:\ \operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\overline U)<r\,\},\qquad \operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\overline U):=\inf\{\lVert\zeta-x\rVert:x\in\overline U\},$$

where $\overline U$ is the closure of $U$ in $\mathbb R^{2d}$ and the norm is the Euclidean norm of $\mathbb C^{2d}\cong\mathbb R^{4d}$. Each $D(r)$ is open, contains $U$, and $D(r)\subseteq D(r')$ for $r\le r'$; if $U$ is star-shaped with respect to $0$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), then every $D(r)$ is star-shaped with respect to $0$ as well.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$.

derivations.claim: Lipschitz estimate. For $W\in B(Z_0,3s/4)$ and each $k$, the polydisc $\Delta_{s/4}(W)$ is contained in $\Delta_s(Z_0)\subseteq D$: a point $\zeta$ of it has $|\zeta_k-W_k|<s/4$, so $|\zeta_k-Z_0{}_k|<s/4+3s/4=s$. Hence by [L1] applied to the holomorphic $F$ at $W$ with polyradius $s/4$, $\lVert\partial_{z_k}F(W)\rVert\le 4M/s$; consequently for $W,W'\in B(Z_0,3s/4)$ the mean value estimate along the segment (which lies in the convex ball by [L6]) gives $\lVert F(W)-F(W')\rVert\le 4nM\lVert W-W'\rVert/s=:\Lambda\lVert W-W'\rVert$ with $\Lambda=4nM/s=1/(2t_0)$.

The Picard map [construct]. Fix $Z\in B(Z_0,s/4)$ and let $X_Z$ be the set of continuous $\gamma:D_{t_0}\to\mathbb C^n$ with $\gamma(0)=Z$ and $\lVert\gamma(t)-Z\rVert\le s/2$ for all $t\in D_{t_0}$, equipped with the supremum distance. Define $T\gamma$ by $(T\gamma)(t):=Z+t\int_0^1F(\gamma(\sigma t))\,d\sigma$. For $\gamma\in X_Z$ the integrand is continuous and its values lie in $B(Z,s/2)\subseteq B(Z_0,3s/4)$ by [L6], so $\lVert(T\gamma)(t)-Z\rVert\le|t|M\le t_0M=s/(8n)\le s/2$: $T$ maps $X_Z$ to itself. Moreover by step 1.1, for $\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in X_Z$, $$\lVert(T\gamma_1)(t)-(T\gamma_2)(t)\rVert\le|t|\int_0^1\Lambda\lVert\gamma_1(\sigma t)-\gamma_2(\sigma t)\rVert\,d\sigma\le t_0\Lambda\lVert\gamma_1-\gamma_2\rVert_\infty=\tfrac12\lVert\gamma_1-\gamma_2\rVert_\infty.$$

Iterates. Put $\gamma_0(t):=Z$ and $\gamma_{m+1}:=T\gamma_m$; all $\gamma_m$ lie in $X_Z$ by step 2.1, and $\lVert\gamma_{m+1}-\gamma_m\rVert_\infty\le2^{-m}\lVert\gamma_1-\gamma_0\rVert_\infty\le2^{-m}t_0M$. Each $\gamma_m$ is continuous, and is holomorphic on $D_{t_0}$ in the variable $t$: $\gamma_0$ is constant; if $\gamma_m$ is holomorphic then $\sigma\mapsto\gamma_m(\sigma t)$ is holomorphic in $t$ for each $\sigma$ by [L2], so $\sigma\mapsto F(\gamma_m(\sigma t))$ is jointly continuous in $(\sigma,t)$ and holomorphic in $t$, and its $\sigma$-integral is holomorphic in $t$ by [L3]; multiplying by $t$ gives $T\gamma_m$ holomorphic. Moreover, for fixed $t$ each $\gamma_m(t,\cdot)$ is holomorphic in $Z$ on $B(Z_0,s/4)$: the same induction, with [L3] applied in each $Z$-coordinate and [[lem-cm-cauchy-formula-and-power-series-on-polydiscs]] upgrading separate holomorphy plus continuity to holomorphy.

Uniform convergence. By step 3.1, $(\gamma_m)$ is uniformly Cauchy on $D_{t_0}\times B(Z_0,s/4)$: $\lVert\gamma_{m'}-\gamma_m\rVert_\infty\le2^{-m+1}t_0M$ for $m'\ge m$. Hence it converges uniformly to a map $\Phi$ on the product, which is therefore continuous by [L4] and satisfies $\lVert\Phi(t,Z)-Z\rVert\le s/2$, indeed $\le M|t|\le s/(8n)$; $\Phi(0,Z)=Z$. For fixed $Z$, applying [L4] to the one-variable functions $t\mapsto\gamma_m(t,Z)$ shows $t\mapsto\Phi(t,Z)$ is holomorphic on $\{|t|<t_0\}$; for fixed $t$, applying [L4] in each complex coordinate of $Z$ shows $Z\mapsto\Phi(t,Z)$ is holomorphic in each variable separately, and then [[lem-cm-cauchy-formula-and-power-series-on-polydiscs]] upgrades continuity plus separate holomorphy to holomorphy on $\{|t|<t_0\}\times B(Z_0,s/4)$.

Fixed point. $T$ is Lipschitz with constant $1/2$ on $X_Z$ by step 2.1, so $T\Phi=\lim_mT\gamma_m=\lim_m\gamma_{m+1}=\Phi$ uniformly. Hence $\Phi(t,Z)=Z+t\int_0^1F(\Phi(\sigma t,Z))\,d\sigma=Z+\int_0^tF(\Phi(\tau,Z))\,d\tau$ for all $(t,Z)$, the last integral being the segment integral. Differentiating: for $h\ne0$ small, $$\frac{\Phi(t+h,Z)-\Phi(t,Z)}{h}-F(\Phi(t,Z))=\int_0^1\bigl[F(\Phi(t+\sigma h,Z))-F(\Phi(t,Z))\bigr]d\sigma\longrightarrow0$$ as $h\to0$ by continuity of $\Phi$ and $F$ and the norm inequality [L5]. Hence $\frac{d}{dt}\Phi(t,Z)=F(\Phi(t,Z))$; with $\Phi(0,Z)=Z$ and the displacement bound this proves clause 1 except uniqueness, and clause 2.

Uniqueness and composition. Two solutions in the prescribed curve ball obey the contraction inequality of step 2.1 and coincide. More generally, two local solutions through any point agree on a sufficiently small time disc by that same argument centred at the point; the set of times of agreement is both relatively open and closed in a connected common continuation, hence they agree there. For fixed $s_1$, the curves $t\mapsto\Phi(s_1+t,Z)$ and $t\mapsto\Phi(t,\Phi(s_1,Z))$ have the same initial value and derivative $F$ wherever both are defined. Local uniqueness, followed by this continuation argument, proves the qualified composition rule and, with $t=-s_1$, the inverse rule. This proves all three clauses.

Let $m\ge1$, let $a\in\mathbb C^m$, let $\rho$ be a polyradius with $0<\rho_k<\infty$, and let $f:\Delta_\rho(a)\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and holomorphic in each variable separately, that is, for every $k$ and every choice of the other coordinates the slice $\zeta\mapsto f(\dots,\zeta,\dots)$ is holomorphic on its open disc ([[def-cm-complex-phase-domains-and-holomorphic-maps]], [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]). For a polyradius $r$ with $r_k<\rho_k$ put $M(r):=\sup_{\Gamma_r(a)}|f|$, a finite number.

Then:

1. **Iterated Cauchy formula.** For every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$,
 $$f(z)=\frac{1}{(2\pi i)^m}\oint_{|\zeta_1-a_1|=r_1}\cdots\oint_{|\zeta_m-a_m|=r_m}\frac{f(\zeta)}{\prod_{k}(\zeta_k-z_k)}\,d\zeta_1\cdots d\zeta_m,$$
 and the iterated integrals in any order of the variables agree.
2. **Power-series expansion.** For every polyradius $r'$ with $r_k<r'_k<\rho_k$, and every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$,
 $$f(z)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N^m}c_\alpha\,(z-a)^\alpha,\qquad c_\alpha=\frac{1}{(2\pi i)^m}\oint_{\Gamma_{r'}(a)}\frac{f(\zeta)\,d\zeta}{(\zeta-a)^{\alpha+\mathbf 1}},$$
 where the coefficients $c_\alpha$ do not depend on $r'$, the series converges absolutely and uniformly on every compact subset of $\Delta_\rho(a)$, and $|c_\alpha|\le M(r')\prod_k (r'_k)^{-\alpha_k}$.
3. **Holomorphy, derivatives and estimates.** The function $f$ is holomorphic on $\Delta_\rho(a)$ in the sense of [[def-cm-complex-phase-domains-and-holomorphic-maps]]. Its coordinate derivatives $\partial_{z_k}f$ exist everywhere on $\Delta_\rho(a)$, are continuous and holomorphic in each variable separately there, and satisfy, for $0<s_k<\rho_k$,
 $$|\partial_{z_k}f(a)|\le\frac{M(s)}{s_k}.$$

Let $m,l,p\ge1$ and let $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$, $D'\subseteq\mathbb C^l$ be open, with holomorphy in the sense of [[def-cm-complex-phase-domains-and-holomorphic-maps]].

1. **Chain rule.** If $g:D'\to D$ and $F:D\to\mathbb C^p$ are holomorphic, then $F\circ g:D'\to\mathbb C^p$ is holomorphic and
 $$D(F\circ g)(z)=DF\bigl(g(z)\bigr)\circ Dg(z)\qquad(z\in D').$$
2. **Wirtinger derivatives and the bracket matrix.** If $f:D\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, then $f$ is totally differentiable as a map of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ and, writing $x_k,y_k$ for the real and imaginary parts of $z_k$,
 $$\partial_{\bar z_k}f:=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_{x_k}f+i\,\partial_{y_k}f\bigr)=0,\qquad \partial_{z_k}f:=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_{x_k}f-i\,\partial_{y_k}f\bigr)=Df(e_k).$$
 Consequently, for holomorphic $f,g$ on a complex phase domain $D\subseteq\mathbb C^{2d}$, with $\nabla f=(\partial_{z^1}f,\dots,\partial_{w_d}f)$ and $J$ the standard matrix,
 $$\{f,g\}=(\nabla f)^{\mathsf T}J\,\nabla g.$$
3. **Coefficient extraction in a complex step variable.** Let $0<\sigma\le\infty$ and let $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, and let $F:\{|h|<\sigma\}\times D\to\mathbb C^p$ be holomorphic. Then for every $j\in\mathbb N$ the coefficient map
 $$c_j(z):=\partial_h^jF(0,z)/j!$$
 is holomorphic on $D$, and for every $0<s<\sigma$, $c_j(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|h|=s}\frac{F(h,z)}{h^{j+1}}\,dh$.
4. **Locally uniform limits.** If $F_n:D\to\mathbb C^p$ are holomorphic and $F_n\to F$ locally uniformly on $D$ in the sense of [[rem-locally-uniform-convergence-dictionary]] and [[def-uniform-convergence-of-complex-valued-functions]], then $F$ is holomorphic on $D$.

**Holomorphic maps.** Let $m,p\ge1$ and let $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, identified with an open subset of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ through $\mathbb C^m\cong\mathbb R^{2m}$. A map $F:D\to\mathbb C^p$ is **complex differentiable at** $a\in D$ when there is a map $L:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C^p$ that is $\mathbb C$-linear — $L(u+v)=L(u)+L(v)$ and $L(\lambda u)=\lambda L(u)$ for $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ ([[def-linear-map]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) — with

$$F(a+v)=F(a)+L(v)+r(v),\qquad \frac{\lVert r(v)\rVert}{\lVert v\rVert}\longrightarrow0\ \ (v\to0),$$

the norm being the Euclidean norm of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ and $\mathbb R^{2p}$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]). Such an $L$ is unique by the argument of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]], applied componentwise; it is denoted $DF(a)$. The map $F$ is **holomorphic on** $D$ when it is complex differentiable at every point of $D$; for $m=p=1$ this is the notion of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]. For holomorphic $F$ and $k\le m$ put $\partial_{z_k}F(a):=DF(a)(e_k)$, the $k$-th coordinate derivative; for $p=1$ this is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] in the complex coordinate direction.

**Real analytic functions.** Let $N\ge1$ and let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^N$ be open. A function $\varphi:V\to\mathbb R$ is **real analytic at** $x\in V$ when there are an open set $W\subseteq\mathbb C^N$ with $x\in W$ and a holomorphic $F:W\to\mathbb C$ with $F(\xi)=\varphi(\xi)$ for every $\xi\in W\cap V$; $\varphi$ is **real analytic on** $V$ when it is real analytic at every point of $V$. Thus real analyticity is defined here exactly as *admitting a local holomorphic extension*.

**Polydiscs.** For $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $\rho=(\rho_1,\dots,\rho_m)$ with $0<\rho_k\le\infty$ put

$$\Delta_\rho(a):=\{\,z\in\mathbb C^m:\ |z_k-a_k|<\rho_k\ \text{for all }k\,\},\qquad \Gamma_\rho(a):=\{\,z:\ |z_k-a_k|=\rho_k\ \text{for all }k\,\},$$

the open **polydisc** and its **distinguished boundary**; a polydisc is open and convex ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metric-topology]]).

**Complex phase domains.** Let $d\ge1$. A **complex phase domain** is a nonempty open $D\subseteq\mathbb C^{2d}$ whose points are written $Z=(z,w)$ with $z=(z^1,\dots,z^d)$, $w=(w_1,\dots,w_d)\in\mathbb C^d$. On it define the **complexified canonical two-form** and the **complexified Poisson bracket** of holomorphic functions $f,g:D\to\mathbb C$ by

$$\omega_{\mathbb C}:=\sum_{i=1}^d dz^i\wedge dw_i,\qquad \{f,g\}:=\sum_{i=1}^d\bigl(\partial_{z^i}f\,\partial_{w_i}g-\partial_{w_i}f\,\partial_{z^i}g\bigr),$$

and for a holomorphic $f:D\to\mathbb C$ its **complex Hamiltonian field** $X_f:=J\nabla f$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0_d&I_d\\-I_d&0_d\end{pmatrix}$ is the standard symplectic matrix of [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]] and $\nabla f=(\partial_{z^1}f,\dots,\partial_{z^d}f,\partial_{w_1}f,\dots,\partial_{w_d}f)$ is the gradient column of coordinate derivatives. The real subspace $\mathbb R^{2d}\subseteq\mathbb C^{2d}$ and the restriction of $\omega_{\mathbb C}$, $J$ and $\{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\}$ to real-valued functions reproduce the real objects of [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]].

**Distance domains.** For $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{2d}$ and $r>0$ put

$$D(r):=\{\,\zeta\in\mathbb C^{2d}:\ \operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\overline U)<r\,\},\qquad \operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\overline U):=\inf\{\lVert\zeta-x\rVert:x\in\overline U\},$$

where $\overline U$ is the closure of $U$ in $\mathbb R^{2d}$ and the norm is the Euclidean norm of $\mathbb C^{2d}\cong\mathbb R^{4d}$. Each $D(r)$ is open, contains $U$, and $D(r)\subseteq D(r')$ for $r\le r'$; if $U$ is star-shaped with respect to $0$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), then every $D(r)$ is star-shaped with respect to $0$ as well.
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $m,l,p\ge1$ and let $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$, $D'\subseteq\mathbb C^l$ be open, with holomorphy in the sense of [[def-cm-complex-phase-domains-and-holomorphic-maps]].

1. **Chain rule.** If $g:D'\to D$ and $F:D\to\mathbb C^p$ are holomorphic, then $F\circ g:D'\to\mathbb C^p$ is holomorphic and
 $$D(F\circ g)(z)=DF\bigl(g(z)\bigr)\circ Dg(z)\qquad(z\in D').$$
2. **Wirtinger derivatives and the bracket matrix.** If $f:D\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, then $f$ is totally differentiable as a map of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ and, writing $x_k,y_k$ for the real and imaginary parts of $z_k$,
 $$\partial_{\bar z_k}f:=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_{x_k}f+i\,\partial_{y_k}f\bigr)=0,\qquad \partial_{z_k}f:=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_{x_k}f-i\,\partial_{y_k}f\bigr)=Df(e_k).$$
 Consequently, for holomorphic $f,g$ on a complex phase domain $D\subseteq\mathbb C^{2d}$, with $\nabla f=(\partial_{z^1}f,\dots,\partial_{w_d}f)$ and $J$ the standard matrix,
 $$\{f,g\}=(\nabla f)^{\mathsf T}J\,\nabla g.$$
3. **Coefficient extraction in a complex step variable.** Let $0<\sigma\le\infty$ and let $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, and let $F:\{|h|<\sigma\}\times D\to\mathbb C^p$ be holomorphic. Then for every $j\in\mathbb N$ the coefficient map
 $$c_j(z):=\partial_h^jF(0,z)/j!$$
 is holomorphic on $D$, and for every $0<s<\sigma$, $c_j(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|h|=s}\frac{F(h,z)}{h^{j+1}}\,dh$.
4. **Locally uniform limits.** If $F_n:D\to\mathbb C^p$ are holomorphic and $F_n\to F$ locally uniformly on $D$ in the sense of [[rem-locally-uniform-convergence-dictionary]] and [[def-uniform-convergence-of-complex-valued-functions]], then $F$ is holomorphic on $D$.
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

**Holomorphic maps.** Let $m,p\ge1$ and let $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, identified with an open subset of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ through $\mathbb C^m\cong\mathbb R^{2m}$. A map $F:D\to\mathbb C^p$ is **complex differentiable at** $a\in D$ when there is a map $L:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C^p$ that is $\mathbb C$-linear — $L(u+v)=L(u)+L(v)$ and $L(\lambda u)=\lambda L(u)$ for $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ ([[def-linear-map]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) — with

$$F(a+v)=F(a)+L(v)+r(v),\qquad \frac{\lVert r(v)\rVert}{\lVert v\rVert}\longrightarrow0\ \ (v\to0),$$

the norm being the Euclidean norm of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ and $\mathbb R^{2p}$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]). Such an $L$ is unique by the argument of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]], applied componentwise; it is denoted $DF(a)$. The map $F$ is **holomorphic on** $D$ when it is complex differentiable at every point of $D$; for $m=p=1$ this is the notion of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]. **Real analytic functions.** Let $N\ge1$ and let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^N$ be open. A function $\varphi:V\to\mathbb R$ is **real analytic at** $x\in V$ when there are an open set $W\subseteq\mathbb C^N$ with $x\in W$ and a holomorphic $F:W\to\mathbb C$ with $F(\xi)=\varphi(\xi)$ for every $\xi\in W\cap V$; $\varphi$ is **real analytic on** $V$ when it is real analytic at every point of $V$. Thus real analyticity is defined here exactly as *admitting a local holomorphic extension*.

**Polydiscs.** For $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $\rho=(\rho_1,\dots,\rho_m)$ with $0<\rho_k\le\infty$ put

$$\Delta_\rho(a):=\{\,z\in\mathbb C^m:\ |z_k-a_k|<\rho_k\ \text{for all }k\,\},\qquad \Gamma_\rho(a):=\{\,z:\ |z_k-a_k|=\rho_k\ \text{for all }k\,\},$$

**Complex phase domains.** Let $d\ge1$. The real subspace $\mathbb R^{2d}\subseteq\mathbb C^{2d}$ and the restriction of $\omega_{\mathbb C}$, $J$ and $\{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\}$ to real-valued functions reproduce the real objects of [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]].

**Distance domains.** For $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{2d}$ and $r>0$ put

$$D(r):=\{\,\zeta\in\mathbb C^{2d}:\ \operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\overline U)<r\,\},\qquad \operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\overline U):=\inf\{\lVert\zeta-x\rVert:x\in\overline U\},$$

where $\overline U$ is the closure of $U$ in $\mathbb R^{2d}$ and the norm is the Euclidean norm of $\mathbb C^{2d}\cong\mathbb R^{4d}$. Each $D(r)$ is open, contains $U$, and $D(r)\subseteq D(r')$ for $r\le r'$; if $U$ is star-shaped with respect to $0$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), then every $D(r)$ is star-shaped with respect to $0$ as well.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For $A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, the **transpose** of $A$ is the matrix
$A^{\mathsf T}\in M_{n\times m}(F)$ defined by

$$(A^{\mathsf T})_{ji}:=a_{ij}.$$

Thus transposition interchanges rows and columns. The transpose of a zero-sized
matrix is the unique matrix of the transposed zero-sized shape.

A matrix $A\in M_n(F)$ is **invertible** when there is a matrix $B\in M_n(F)$
such that

$$AB=I_n=BA.$$

Such a $B$ is unique and is denoted $A^{-1}$. The **general linear set** is

$$\operatorname{GL}_n(F):=\{A\in M_n(F):A\text{ is invertible}\}.$$

It is the set of units of the ring $M_n(F)$. The fact that it is a group under
matrix multiplication is [[cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group]]. For $n=0$,
the unique empty matrix is $I_0$ and is its own inverse.

Let $m,l,p\ge1$ and let $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$, $D'\subseteq\mathbb C^l$ be open, with holomorphy in the sense of [[def-cm-complex-phase-domains-and-holomorphic-maps]].

1. **Chain rule.** If $g:D'\to D$ and $F:D\to\mathbb C^p$ are holomorphic, then $F\circ g:D'\to\mathbb C^p$ is holomorphic and
 $$D(F\circ g)(z)=DF\bigl(g(z)\bigr)\circ Dg(z)\qquad(z\in D').$$
2. **Wirtinger derivatives and the bracket matrix.** If $f:D\to\mathbb C$ is holomorphic, then $f$ is totally differentiable as a map of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ and, writing $x_k,y_k$ for the real and imaginary parts of $z_k$,
 $$\partial_{\bar z_k}f:=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_{x_k}f+i\,\partial_{y_k}f\bigr)=0,\qquad \partial_{z_k}f:=\tfrac12\bigl(\partial_{x_k}f-i\,\partial_{y_k}f\bigr)=Df(e_k).$$
 Consequently, for holomorphic $f,g$ on a complex phase domain $D\subseteq\mathbb C^{2d}$, with $\nabla f=(\partial_{z^1}f,\dots,\partial_{w_d}f)$ and $J$ the standard matrix,
 $$\{f,g\}=(\nabla f)^{\mathsf T}J\,\nabla g.$$

 $$c_j(z):=\partial_h^jF(0,z)/j!$$
 is holomorphic on $D$, and for every $0<s<\sigma$, $c_j(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|h|=s}\frac{F(h,z)}{h^{j+1}}\,dh$.

derivations.claim: The derivative of the matrix identity along the flow. Fix $(Z,t)$ in the flow domain and put $A(\tau):=D\varphi^\tau_F(Z)$. By [L2], $A'(\tau)=DX_F(\varphi^\tau_F(Z))A(\tau)$, and by [L3], $DX_F=J\operatorname{Hess}F$ with $\operatorname{Hess}F$ symmetric. Then $$\frac{d}{d\tau}\bigl(A(\tau)^{\mathsf T}JA(\tau)\bigr)=A^{\mathsf T}\bigl[(J\operatorname{Hess}F)^{\mathsf T}J+J(J\operatorname{Hess}F)\bigr]A= A^{\mathsf T}\bigl[\operatorname{Hess}F^{\mathsf T}J^{\mathsf T}J+J^2\operatorname{Hess}F\bigr]A=0,$$ using $J^{\mathsf T}J=I$, $J^2=-I$ and $\operatorname{Hess}F^{\mathsf T}=\operatorname{Hess}F$ ([L4]). Since the expression is continuous in $\tau$ and has zero derivative on the connected flow interval, it equals its value at $\tau=0$, namely $I^{\mathsf T}JI=J$. Thus $D\varphi^t_F(Z)^{\mathsf T}JD\varphi^t_F(Z)=J$.

Invertibility. The flow has a two-sided inverse $\varphi^{-t}_F$ ([[lem-cm-complex-analytic-flow-existence-and-holomorphy]], clause 3), so the chain rule gives $D\varphi^{-t}_F(\varphi^t_F(Z))\circ D\varphi^t_F(Z)=I$: the derivative is invertible with inverse $D\varphi^{-t}_F(\varphi^t_F(Z))$, and the identity of step 1.1 transfers to $AJA^{\mathsf T}=J$ by [L4].

Composition. The chain rule gives $D\Psi_h(Z)=A_1A_2A_3$ with $A_1=D\varphi_{\tilde A}^{h/2}$ at $\varphi_{\tilde B}^h(\varphi_{\tilde A}^{h/2}(Z))$, $A_2=D\varphi_{\tilde B}^h$ at $\varphi_{\tilde A}^{h/2}(Z)$ and $A_3=D\varphi_{\tilde A}^{h/2}$ at $Z$. Each $A_i$ satisfies $A_i^{\mathsf T}JA_i=J$ by step 1.1 and is invertible by step 2.1; hence $D\Psi_h(Z)^{\mathsf T}JD\Psi_h(Z)=A_3^{\mathsf T}(A_2^{\mathsf T}(A_1^{\mathsf T}JA_1)A_2)A_3=J$ by [L4], and $D\Psi_h(Z)$ is invertible as a product of invertible matrices.

Bracket identity. Let $f,g$ be holomorphic near $\Psi_h(Z)$. By the chain rule, $
abla(f\circ\Psi_h)(Z)=D\Psi_h(Z)^{\mathsf T}
abla f(\Psi_h(Z))$, and likewise for $g$; hence by [L5] $$\{f\circ\Psi_h,g\circ\Psi_h\}(Z)=
abla f(\Psi_h(Z))^{\mathsf T} igl(D\Psi_h(Z)\,J\,D\Psi_h(Z)^{\mathsf T} igr)
abla g(\Psi_h(Z)).$$ By step 3.1 and the equivalence of [L4] (applicable because $D\Psi_h(Z)$ is invertible), $D\Psi_h\,J\,D\Psi_h^{\mathsf T}=J$, so the last display equals $
abla f(\Psi_h(Z))^{\mathsf T}J
abla g(\Psi_h(Z))=\{f,g\}(\Psi_h(Z))$ by [L5] again.
Conclusion. Step 1.1 gives clause 1 for the two fields, step 3.1 gives clause 2, and step 4.1 gives clause 3.

**Holomorphic maps.** Let $m,p\ge1$ and let $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, identified with an open subset of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ through $\mathbb C^m\cong\mathbb R^{2m}$. A map $F:D\to\mathbb C^p$ is **complex differentiable at** $a\in D$ when there is a map $L:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C^p$ that is $\mathbb C$-linear — $L(u+v)=L(u)+L(v)$ and $L(\lambda u)=\lambda L(u)$ for $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ ([[def-linear-map]], [[def-euclidean-linear-map]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) — with

$$F(a+v)=F(a)+L(v)+r(v),\qquad \frac{\lVert r(v)\rVert}{\lVert v\rVert}\longrightarrow0\ \ (v\to0),$$

the norm being the Euclidean norm of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ and $\mathbb R^{2p}$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]). Such an $L$ is unique by the argument of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]], applied componentwise; it is denoted $DF(a)$. The map $F$ is **holomorphic on** $D$ when it is complex differentiable at every point of $D$; for $m=p=1$ this is the notion of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]. For holomorphic $F$ and $k\le m$ put $\partial_{z_k}F(a):=DF(a)(e_k)$, the $k$-th coordinate derivative; for $p=1$ this is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] in the complex coordinate direction.

**Real analytic functions.** Let $N\ge1$ and let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^N$ be open. A function $\varphi:V\to\mathbb R$ is **real analytic at** $x\in V$ when there are an open set $W\subseteq\mathbb C^N$ with $x\in W$ and a holomorphic $F:W\to\mathbb C$ with $F(\xi)=\varphi(\xi)$ for every $\xi\in W\cap V$; $\varphi$ is **real analytic on** $V$ when it is real analytic at every point of $V$. Thus real analyticity is defined here exactly as *admitting a local holomorphic extension*.

**Polydiscs.** For $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $\rho=(\rho_1,\dots,\rho_m)$ with $0<\rho_k\le\infty$ put

$$\Delta_\rho(a):=\{\,z\in\mathbb C^m:\ |z_k-a_k|<\rho_k\ \text{for all }k\,\},\qquad \Gamma_\rho(a):=\{\,z:\ |z_k-a_k|=\rho_k\ \text{for all }k\,\},$$

the open **polydisc** and its **distinguished boundary**; a polydisc is open and convex ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metric-topology]]).

**Complex phase domains.** Let $d\ge1$. A **complex phase domain** is a nonempty open $D\subseteq\mathbb C^{2d}$ whose points are written $Z=(z,w)$ with $z=(z^1,\dots,z^d)$, $w=(w_1,\dots,w_d)\in\mathbb C^d$. On it define the **complexified canonical two-form** and the **complexified Poisson bracket** of holomorphic functions $f,g:D\to\mathbb C$ by

$$\omega_{\mathbb C}:=\sum_{i=1}^d dz^i\wedge dw_i,\qquad \{f,g\}:=\sum_{i=1}^d\bigl(\partial_{z^i}f\,\partial_{w_i}g-\partial_{w_i}f\,\partial_{z^i}g\bigr),$$

and for a holomorphic $f:D\to\mathbb C$ its **complex Hamiltonian field** $X_f:=J\nabla f$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0_d&I_d\\-I_d&0_d\end{pmatrix}$ is the standard symplectic matrix of [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]] and $\nabla f=(\partial_{z^1}f,\dots,\partial_{z^d}f,\partial_{w_1}f,\dots,\partial_{w_d}f)$ is the gradient column of coordinate derivatives. The real subspace $\mathbb R^{2d}\subseteq\mathbb C^{2d}$ and the restriction of $\omega_{\mathbb C}$, $J$ and $\{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\}$ to real-valued functions reproduce the real objects of [[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]].

**Distance domains.** For $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{2d}$ and $r>0$ put

$$D(r):=\{\,\zeta\in\mathbb C^{2d}:\ \operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\overline U)<r\,\},\qquad \operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\overline U):=\inf\{\lVert\zeta-x\rVert:x\in\overline U\},$$

where $\overline U$ is the closure of $U$ in $\mathbb R^{2d}$ and the norm is the Euclidean norm of $\mathbb C^{2d}\cong\mathbb R^{4d}$. Each $D(r)$ is open, contains $U$, and $D(r)\subseteq D(r')$ for $r\le r'$; if $U$ is star-shaped with respect to $0$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), then every $D(r)$ is star-shaped with respect to $0$ as well.

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb C^n$ be holomorphic in the sense of [[def-cm-complex-phase-domains-and-holomorphic-maps]] with $\lVert F\rVert\le M$ everywhere on $D$ for some $M>0$, let $Z_0\in D$ and let $s>0$ satisfy $\Delta_s(Z_0)\subseteq D$ ([[def-cm-complex-phase-domains-and-holomorphic-maps]]). Put

$$t_0:=\frac{s}{8nM},\qquad D_{t_0}:=\{t\in\mathbb C:\ |t|\le t_0\}.$$

Then there is a map $\Phi:D_{t_0}\times B(Z_0,s/4)\to D$ such that:

1. **Solution.** For every $Z\in B(Z_0,s/4)$ the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t,Z)$ is the unique solution of $\frac{d}{d\tau}Y(\tau)=F(Y(\tau))$, $Y(0)=Z$, on $D_{t_0}$ among all solutions with values in the ball $B(Z,s/2)$; it satisfies $\lVert\Phi(t,Z)-Z\rVert\le M|t|$ and $\|\Phi(t,Z)-Z\|\le s/(8n)$.
2. **Holomorphy.** $\Phi$ is holomorphic on the open set $\{|t|<t_0\}\times B(Z_0,s/4)$ in the sense of [[def-cm-complex-phase-domains-and-holomorphic-maps]], and $\Phi(0,Z)=Z$.
3. **Composition and inverse.** The local solutions glue uniquely on overlapping initial-data balls. For the resulting local flow, whenever both sides are defined on the same connected continuation of the solution, $\Phi(s_2,\Phi(s_1,Z))=\Phi(s_1+s_2,Z)$. In particular, for sufficiently small $s_1$ for which the forward and backward local solutions exist, $\Phi(-s_1,\Phi(s_1,Z))=Z$. No assertion that every translated point remains in the displayed initial-data ball is made.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $(U,U_\rho,\tilde A,\tilde B,M,K,\delta,\Psi_h)$ be analytic splitting data as in [[def-cm-analytic-splitting-data-and-exact-splitting-map]], with $J$ the standard matrix and $\omega_{\mathbb C}$, $\{\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\}$ the complexified form and bracket of [[def-cm-complex-phase-domains-and-holomorphic-maps]]. 1. For every $(t,Z)$ in the flow domain, $\varphi_F^t$ is holomorphic near $Z$, its derivative is invertible, and
 $$D\varphi_F^t(Z)^{\mathsf T}J\,D\varphi_F^t(Z)=J.$$
2. For every $h$ and every point $Z$ where $\Psi_h$ is defined and holomorphic, $D\Psi_h(Z)$ is invertible and
 $$D\Psi_h(Z)^{\mathsf T}J\,D\Psi_h(Z)=J.$$
3. For all holomorphic $f,g$ on an open set containing $\Psi_h(Z)$,
 $$\{f\circ\Psi_h,\;g\circ\Psi_h\}(Z)=\{f,g\}\bigl(\Psi_h(Z)\bigr).$$

1. **Chain rule.** If $g:D'\to D$ and $F:D\to\mathbb C^p$ are holomorphic, then $F\circ g:D'\to\mathbb C^p$ is holomorphic and

 Consequently, for holomorphic $f,g$ on a complex phase domain $D\subseteq\mathbb C^{2d}$, with $\nabla f=(\partial_{z^1}f,\dots,\partial_{w_d}f)$ and $J$ the standard matrix,
 $$\{f,g\}=(\nabla f)^{\mathsf T}J\,\nabla g.$$
3. **Coefficient extraction in a complex step variable.** Let $0<\sigma\le\infty$ and let $D\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be open, and let $F:\{|h|<\sigma\}\times D\to\mathbb C^p$ be holomorphic. Then for every $j\in\mathbb N$ the coefficient map

 is holomorphic on $D$, and for every $0<s<\sigma$, $c_j(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|h|=s}\frac{F(h,z)}{h^{j+1}}\,dh$.
4. **Locally uniform limits.** If $F_n:D\to\mathbb C^p$ are holomorphic and $F_n\to F$ locally uniformly on $D$ in the sense of [[rem-locally-uniform-convergence-dictionary]] and [[def-uniform-convergence-of-complex-valued-functions]], then $F$ is holomorphic on $D$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $a\in\mathbb C^m$, let $\rho$ be a polyradius with $0<\rho_k<\infty$, and let $f:\Delta_\rho(a)\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and holomorphic in each variable separately, that is, for every $k$ and every choice of the other coordinates the slice $\zeta\mapsto f(\dots,\zeta,\dots)$ is holomorphic on its open disc ([[def-cm-complex-phase-domains-and-holomorphic-maps]], [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]). For a polyradius $r$ with $r_k<\rho_k$ put $M(r):=\sup_{\Gamma_r(a)}|f|$, a finite number.

Then:

1. **Iterated Cauchy formula.** For every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$,
 $$f(z)=\frac{1}{(2\pi i)^m}\oint_{|\zeta_1-a_1|=r_1}\cdots\oint_{|\zeta_m-a_m|=r_m}\frac{f(\zeta)}{\prod_{k}(\zeta_k-z_k)}\,d\zeta_1\cdots d\zeta_m,$$
 and the iterated integrals in any order of the variables agree.
2. **Power-series expansion.** For every polyradius $r'$ with $r_k<r'_k<\rho_k$, and every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$,
 $$f(z)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N^m}c_\alpha\,(z-a)^\alpha,\qquad c_\alpha=\frac{1}{(2\pi i)^m}\oint_{\Gamma_{r'}(a)}\frac{f(\zeta)\,d\zeta}{(\zeta-a)^{\alpha+\mathbf 1}},$$
 where the coefficients $c_\alpha$ do not depend on $r'$, the series converges absolutely and uniformly on every compact subset of $\Delta_\rho(a)$, and $|c_\alpha|\le M(r')\prod_k (r'_k)^{-\alpha_k}$.

Its coordinate derivatives $\partial_{z_k}f$ exist everywhere on $\Delta_\rho(a)$, are continuous and holomorphic in each variable separately there, and satisfy, for $0<s_k<\rho_k$,
 $$|\partial_{z_k}f(a)|\le\frac{M(s)}{s_k}.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

$$D(r):=\{\,\zeta\in\mathbb C^{2d}:\ \operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\overline U)<r\,\},\qquad \operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\overline U):=\inf\{\lVert\zeta-x\rVert:x\in\overline U\},$$

where $\overline U$ is the closure of $U$ in $\mathbb R^{2d}$ and the norm is the Euclidean norm of $\mathbb C^{2d}\cong\mathbb R^{4d}$. Each $D(r)$ is open, contains $U$, and $D(r)\subseteq D(r')$ for $r\le r'$; if $U$ is star-shaped with respect to $0$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), then every $D(r)$ is star-shaped with respect to $0$ as well.

derivations.claim: Margin bookkeeping. Fix $N\ge2$, $k\le N$ and $Z\in D_k$, so $\operatorname{dist}(Z,\overline U)<\rho/2-2bk$. Put $\xi:=\Psi_h(Z)$. If $2M|h|\le b$ then by [F1] and [F2] $\operatorname{dist}(\xi,\overline U)\le\operatorname{dist}(Z,\overline U)+\lVert\xi-Z\rVert<\rho/2-2bk+b=\rho/2-2b(k-1)-b$, so $\xi\in D_{k-1}$ with margin at least $b$; moreover every point $\zeta$ of the segment from $Z$ to $\xi$ has $\operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\overline U)<\rho/2-2b(k-1)-b$, and then the polydisc $\Delta_{(b/\sqrt{2d})\mathbf 1}(\zeta)$ is contained in $B(\zeta,b)\subseteq D_{k-1}$. The entire composition can be constructed using polydiscs of radius $\rho/(4\sqrt{2d})$ centred at each intermediate point: they lie in $U_\rho$ since these points stay within $b$ of $D_0$. The flow lemma permits each subtime when $|h|\le\rho/(64d\sqrt{2d}M)$, which follows from $N\ge2$ and $C_0\ge128d^2$. Thus the displacement estimate is available without circularly assuming flow existence. Finally the intermediate points of the three-flow composition are within $\lVert\Psi_h(Z)-Z\rVert\le b$ of $Z$ by [F2], so all flows are applied to points of $D_{k-1}$ with the margins required by [F2]. The step bound $2M|h|\le b$ holds whenever $2M|h|\le\rho/(8N)$, i.e. for $|h|\le r_N=\rho/(C_0MN)$ as soon as $C_0\ge16$.

Single-step bound. Let $f$ be holomorphic on $D_{k-1}$ with $|f|\le F$. For $Z\in D_k$, $\xi=\Psi_h(Z)$ and $\zeta$ on the segment, [F3] applied at $\zeta$ with the polyradius $(b/\sqrt{2d})\mathbf 1$, whose distinguished boundary lies in $D_{k-1}$ by step 1.1, gives $|\partial_{z_k}f(\zeta)|\le\sqrt{2d}\,F/b$ for every $k$. Hence by [F4], $$\lvert f(\xi)-f(Z)\rvert\le\sqrt{2d}\cdot\sqrt{2d}\cdot\frac{F}{b}\cdot\lVert\xi-Z\rVert\le\frac{2d\,F}{b}\cdot2M|h|,$$ and $\Delta_hf$ is holomorphic on $D_k$ by [F5]. This is clause 2 with $C_d:=4d^2$, which depends only on $d$.

Iteration. By induction on $k$: suppose $\Delta_h^{k-1}f$ is holomorphic on $D_{k-1}$ with $|\Delta_h^{k-1}f|\le q^{k-1}|f|_{D_0}$ (true for $k=1$), then step 1.1 shows $\Psi_h(D_k)\subseteq D_{k-1}$, so $\Delta_h^kf=\Delta_h(\Delta_h^{k-1}f)$ is defined and holomorphic on $D_k$ by clause 2, with bound $q\cdot q^{k-1}|f|_{D_0}=q^k|f|_{D_0}$.

The factor $q$. With $C_0\ge16$ the constraint $|h|\le r_N$ implies $2M|h|\le\rho/(8N)=b$ and, with the constant $C_d=4d^2$ of step 2.1, $$q=\frac{4d^2M|h|}{b}\le\frac{4d^2M\rho}{C_0MN}\cdot\frac{8N}{\rho}=\frac{32d^2}{C_0}\le\frac14,$$ because $C_0\ge128d^2=32C_d$. This proves clause 3 with $q\le1/4$.
Conclusion. Clause 1 is step 1.1, clause 2 is step 2.1, clause 3 is steps 3.1 and 4.1; all constants depend only on $d$, $M$, $\rho$.
